title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning
authors: Sepehr Mousavi, Levi Lingsch, Siddhartha Mishra, Laura De Lorenzis
abstract: Neural operators fit their representation of functions to the task they are trained on, so every new task rebuilds a reduced space from labeled data. Following the self-supervised pre-training that made representations shareable in natural language processing and computer vision, we decouple representation learning from operator learning. A functional autoencoder is pre-trained on analytic functions synthesized on the fly, with no solver and no labels, to represent functions on arbitrary point clouds, and the latent space it induces is frozen and reused across tasks. The representation is exactly equivariant to translation, dilation, and amplitude, and reconstructs solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) and natural images on geometries it never saw. Being task-agnostic, the latent space can be interpreted in its own right. The whole space is used and decodes to valid fields, it preserves the ordering of distances between physical fields, its geodesics interpolate physical evolutions, and edit directions transfer across fields. With frozen representation maps, a dataset is encoded once and a neural operator is trained entirely on cached embeddings, which saves memory and training time. On 28 tasks in fluid dynamics, solid mechanics, acoustics, and the Helmholtz and Poisson equations, this paradigm can exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art end-to-end architectures, with up to an order of magnitude higher throughput and memory savings that fit models nearly two orders of magnitude larger on consumer-grade GPUs. At inference, latent rollouts run up to an order of magnitude faster than regular rollouts, and chunked inference processes functions of over half a billion points on a single consumer-grade GPU.

infographic.key_insight: A self-supervised functional autoencoder learns a reusable, task-agnostic latent space, separating function representation from neural operator training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solid-mechanics surrogates, frozen representations can reduce operator-training memory and time while supporting fields sampled on arbitrary point clouds.
method: Pre-train a functional autoencoder on analytic functions synthesized without solvers or labels.
Freeze translation-, dilation-, and amplitude-equivariant representation maps, then train operators on cached embeddings.
Run predictions and rollouts in latent space, with chunked decoding for large fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 28 tasks spanning solid mechanics, fluids, acoustics, Helmholtz, and Poisson equations, the abstract reports accuracy that can exceed state-of-the-art end-to-end models, up to an order-of-magnitude higher throughput, and inference on over half a billion points using one consumer-grade GPU.
infographic.watch_item: For engineering deployment, validate transfer accuracy and physical fidelity on the intended geometries, boundary conditions, and material regimes; aggregate benchmarks do not guarantee reliability for every mechanics problem.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Supervised Learning of Universal Latent Spaces for Operator Learning

title: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev-Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics
authors: Juan José Rodríguez-Aldavero, Ángel de la Rosa Velasco, Juan José García-Ripoll
abstract: Quantum-inspired numerical methods for partial differential equations represent discretized fields and operators as quantics tensor trains (QTT), so that their cost depends on how compressible the problem is rather than on the number of unknowns. Global spectral formulations in this setting have so far relied on Fourier bases, restricted to periodic problems, or on collocation, which does not preserve the variational structure exploited by tensor-network solvers. We introduce a QTT Chebyshev-Galerkin method that assembles and solves global spectral systems directly in compressed form, without forming the underlying arrays. Starting from the weak formulation, the method handles coupled elliptic systems with variable coefficients, smoothly mapped geometries, and mixed Dirichlet-Robin boundary conditions, and yields symmetric positive-definite systems suited to variational tensor-network solvers. Parameters and random inputs enter as additional coordinates, so the same construction returns the solution over an entire parameter space in a single solve. In linear elasticity, the method retains spectral convergence and reaches errors below $10^{-8}$ on a three-dimensional benchmark, beyond those attained by QTT finite differences and Q2/Q4 FEniCSx finite elements over the tested range. A six-parameter cantilever design study covering $1.7\times10^{7}$ designs is solved in a single 92s run, and a stochastic problem with ten random coordinates is represented with $2.4\times10^{6}$ times less memory than its full coefficient array.

infographic.key_insight: A quantics tensor-train (QTT) Chebyshev–Galerkin method solves nonperiodic boundary-value problems directly in compressed form while preserving their variational structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method enables accurate elasticity analysis across large design and uncertainty spaces without storing every field coefficient explicitly.
method: Assemble global Chebyshev–Galerkin systems from the weak formulation directly in QTT form.
Handle variable coefficients, smoothly mapped geometries, and mixed Dirichlet–Robin conditions.
Treat design parameters and random inputs as extra coordinates for a single joint solution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports errors below 10⁻⁸ on a 3D elasticity benchmark, 1.7×10⁷ cantilever designs solved in 92 seconds, and 2.4×10⁶-fold coefficient-storage savings for a ten-random-coordinate problem.
infographic.watch_item: Efficiency depends on tensor compressibility; the reported gains may not carry over to problems requiring high tensor ranks.
infographic.paper_title: A Tensor-Network Chebyshev-Galerkin Method for Boundary-Value Problems in Computational Mechanics

title: Finite Element Elastographic Analysis of Kidney MRI for Computational Assessment of Chronic Kidney Disease
authors: A. Bhattacharjee, M. M. Rahman, A. Srivastava, E. H. Bhuiyan
abstract: Background and Objective: Bridging kidney MRI with patient-specific computational biomechanics may enable accurate, noninvasive assessment of chronic kidney disease. To develop a finite element method (FEM)-based computational elastography framework for estimating renal biomechanical properties from conventional kidney MRI and to evaluate its ability to differentiate chronic kidney disease (CKD) from healthy controls. Methods: Kidney segmentation masks from healthy control and CKD subjects were converted into triangulated surface meshes, and watertight surfaces were tetrahedralized to create volumetric FEM meshes. Kidney tissue was modeled as a nearly incompressible Kelvin-Voigt viscoelastic material. Harmonic wave propagation simulations were performed using FEM, followed by Helmholtz-based elastographic inversion to estimate complex shear modulus distributions. Derived biomechanical parameters were used for CKD classification using machine learning models. Results: FEM-derived stiffness estimates showed consistency with stiffness ranges previously reported in human renal MRE studies and also showed measurable differences between healthy and CKD groups. Machine learning models trained on FEM-derived features achieved classification performance up to 86.26% cross-validation accuracy with an AUC of 0.92. Conclusion: FEM-derived elastographic parameters showed potential for distinguishing CKD from healthy tissue and may provide an alternative for renal biomechanical assessment without dedicated MRE acquisition.

infographic.key_insight: MRI-derived finite element elastography showed potential to distinguish CKD from healthy kidneys without dedicated MRE acquisition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects kidney geometry from conventional MRI to simulated viscoelastic responses and biomechanical features for computational disease assessment.
method: Convert kidney segmentation masks into watertight surfaces and tetrahedral FEM meshes.
Simulate harmonic waves using a nearly incompressible Kelvin–Voigt tissue model.
Estimate complex shear modulus via Helmholtz inversion and classify CKD using machine learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: FEM-derived stiffness was consistent with reported human renal MRE ranges, and classification reached 86.26% cross-validation accuracy with an AUC of 0.92.
infographic.watch_item: Stiffness is inferred from simulated rather than measured wave fields; the abstract reports no direct patient-level MRE validation.
infographic.paper_title: Finite Element Elastographic Analysis of Kidney MRI for Computational Assessment of Chronic Kidney Disease

title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion
authors: Li Zheng, Simin Chen
abstract: Finite element method (FEM) solvers are foundational to scientific and engineering simulation, yet their susceptibility to \emph{efficiency attacks} remains largely unexplored. An adversary can craft syntactically valid and runnable FEM programs that complete successfully while forcing excessive computational work, enabling computational denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Finding such inputs is challenging because FEM programs occupy a vast, structured space constrained by numerical, geometric, and constitutive requirements. We introduce CloakFEM, a domain-guided LLM-agent framework for automatically generating runnable adversarial FEM programs that amplify solver computation. CloakFEM combines LLM-guided search with an FEM-specific intermediate representation and a deterministic validity gate that enforces runnable constraints. Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM discovers adversarial inputs that substantially amplify solver work while remaining valid and solvable. In the most extreme case, solver iterations increase from 43 to 247,367, a \(5{,}752.72\times\) amplification. CloakFEM outperforms five generic black-box baselines and retains an advantage over evolutionary search under a controlled bounded action space. Cross-solver analysis further reveals both problem-intrinsic and solver-specific sources of vulnerability. Our results uncover an underexplored efficiency-attack surface in FEM solvers and show that runnable FEM programs can serve as adversarial inputs.

infographic.key_insight: CloakFEM generates valid, solvable FEM programs that expose resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities by sharply increasing solver work.
infographic.engineering_relevance: FEM simulation services may need computational safeguards because successful completion does not guarantee reasonable resource use.
method: Use a domain-guided LLM agent to search for adversarial FEM programs.
Represent candidates with an FEM-specific intermediate representation.
Apply a deterministic validity gate to enforce runnable constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, CloakFEM outperformed five generic black-box baselines; the most extreme case increased solver iterations from 43 to 247,367 (5,752.72×).
infographic.watch_item: Iteration amplification is not necessarily proportional to wall-clock slowdown, and vulnerability can depend on the solver and problem.
infographic.paper_title: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D
authors: Tommaso Bevilacqua, Axel Klawonn, Martin Lanser, Adam Wasiak
abstract: Overlapping Schwarz methods are among the most successful domain decomposition preconditioners for large-scale finite element simulations. In this work, the Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW), GDSW$^*$, and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces are studied for three-dimensional high-order finite element method (FEM) and virtual element method (VEM) for the Poisson equation and the equations of linear elasticity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of GDSW-type coarse spaces for polynomial degrees $k\ge 3$ in three dimensions, for either discretization. In 3D VEM, the face degrees of freedom (DOFs) are moments instead of point values. The kernel of the differential operator, which defines the interface values of the GDSW coarse basis functions, must be represented through these moments. The construction is therefore no longer purely algebraic and, without this correction, the coarse level loses its effect for $k\ge 3$. FEM and VEM are tested on hexahedral meshes, and VEM is additionally tested on polyhedral ones. Polynomial degrees up to $k=5$ and runs on up to $4\,096$ subdomains and parallel cores are included in the numerical study. Numerical experiments show scalable iteration counts for all coarse space variants for the Poisson problem, illustrating the expected trade-off between the coarse space size and robustness. Further experiments for linear elasticity confirms that the moment-based construction extends naturally from the scalar to the vector-valued problem.

infographic.key_insight: GDSW-type coarse spaces support scalable high-order 3D Schwarz solvers, but VEM requires moment-based representation of operator kernels to preserve coarse-level effectiveness for k≥3.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These preconditioners enable scalable parallel solution of high-order finite element and virtual element systems for Poisson and linear elasticity problems.
method: Study two-level overlapping additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW, GDSW*, and RGDSW coarse spaces.
Represent operator kernels through face moments when constructing 3D VEM coarse bases.
Evaluate FEM and VEM on hexahedral meshes, plus VEM on polyhedral meshes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests reach polynomial degree k=5 and 4,096 subdomains and parallel cores, showing scalable Poisson iteration counts across all coarse-space variants and extension to linear elasticity.
infographic.watch_item: The VEM construction is not purely algebraic: omitting the face-moment correction makes the coarse level ineffective for k≥3.
infographic.paper_title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 3D

title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks
authors: Manish Kumar Singh, Dominic Kang Jueh Lim, Anson Wen Han Cheong, Adams Wai Kin Kong, Chang Quan Lai
abstract: Current methods of deriving ultrastiff isotropic metamaterials require heuristics or topology optimization, which are highly inefficient and limited by human input. To circumvent this, Physics Informed Neural Networks are applied to analytical equations to systematically solve for plate orientations in closed cell lattices. Following a standardized procedure, the plate orientations were modelled and assembled into geometries resembling quasi random foams for validation via finite element simulations. Closed cell 6-plate geometries were also additively manufactured using LAPIS and experimentally characterized. The results indicate that a minimum of 6 plates is required to constitute an ultrastiff isotropic lattice, 7 plates would return the established plate Cubic Octet structure while 8 to 10 plate geometries did not show significant differences in properties. Despite the introduction of some plate bending due to sub-optimal plate placement strategy, relative stiffness of the PINNs lattices adheres closely to the Hashin Shtrikman upper bound, 90 percent of Hashin Shtrikman upper bound at a relative density of 0.4, and the lattices maintain near isotropic behaviour, achieving a Zener ratio of 0.95 at a relative density of 0.1. Benchmarking results show that specific stiffness of PINNs lattices is higher than the majority of isotropic architectures reported in the literature.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-informed neural networks identify plate orientations for near-isotropic, ultrastiff closed-cell lattices, with six plates found to be the minimum required.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a systematic route to lightweight, stiff architectures with nearly direction-independent mechanical properties.
method: Apply PINNs to analytical equations to solve for plate orientations.
Assemble orientations into quasi-random foam-like geometries and validate using finite element simulations.
Additively manufacture six-plate lattices using LAPIS and characterize them experimentally.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported lattices reach 90% of the Hashin–Shtrikman stiffness upper bound at relative density 0.4 and a near-isotropic Zener ratio of 0.95 at relative density 0.1.
infographic.watch_item: Suboptimal plate placement introduces bending, so orientation solutions alone do not guarantee bound-level stiffness in assembled lattices.
infographic.paper_title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks

title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners for conforming Finite Element Methods on Arbitrarily Agglomerated Meshes
authors: Santiago Badia, Jordi Manyer
abstract: Geometric multigrid methods for conforming finite element discretisations classically require a nested mesh hierarchy, forcing coarse meshes to be conforming, which is unsuitable for general domains. In order to eliminate this geometric constraint, we introduce and analyse a family of multilevel auxiliary space preconditioners. At the first level, a conforming Lagrangian discretisation on a fine simplicial mesh is preconditioned by a non-conforming polytopal discretisation posed on an arbitrarily agglomerated coarse mesh. At the subsequent levels, the coarse problem is solved by a geometric multigrid method for that polytopal discretisation on further agglomerated meshes, so that the whole hierarchy is generated from the fine mesh by agglomeration alone. We consider two polytopal discretisations, a symmetric interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method and a hybrid high-order method. The prolongation operator at the first level is an element-wise interpolation onto the fine mesh followed by nodal averaging, preceded in the hybrid high-order case by a local potential reconstruction. For point-Jacobi and vertex-star patch additive Schwarz smoothers, we prove that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by $O((H/h)^3)$, where $H/h$ is the coarsening ratio, and by $O((H/h)^2)$ for the DG variant with penalty proportional to $H/h$. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, on structured and unstructured meshes with agglomerates generated by automatic clustering algorithms, confirm the robustness of the preconditioners.

infographic.key_insight: Auxiliary-space multigrid preconditioners let conforming finite element solvers use arbitrarily agglomerated coarse meshes without requiring conforming coarse meshes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a flexible route to preconditioning finite element systems on complex engineering geometries.
method: Precondition fine-mesh conforming Lagrange elements using a coarse polytopal DG or hybrid high-order discretisation.
Build subsequent multigrid levels entirely by mesh agglomeration.
Transfer coarse solutions by element-wise interpolation and nodal averaging, with local potential reconstruction for hybrid high-order elements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments in 2D and 3D on structured and unstructured meshes with automatically clustered agglomerates support preconditioner robustness.
infographic.watch_item: The proven condition-number bound grows as O((H/h)^3), improving to O((H/h)^2) for DG with appropriately scaled penalties, so aggressive coarsening warrants care.
infographic.paper_title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners for conforming Finite Element Methods on Arbitrarily Agglomerated Meshes

title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization
authors: Brendan Keith, Dohyun Kim, Boyan Lazarov, Ketan Mittal, Cosmin G. Petra, Mathias R. Schmidt
abstract: This work presents an optimization-based remap approach for arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) hydrodynamics that preserves sharp features and physical bounds while conserving global quantities such as volume, mass, momentum, and total energy. Achieving these properties is the main challenge in remap methods. The presented approach is well-suited for high-order finite element (FE) discretizations and ALE methods that allow for large, purely Lagrangian displacements between successive remeshing and remapping steps. Recent advances in parallel, GPU-capable interpolation routines enable the initial transfer of all fields via direct physical-space interpolation, avoiding computationally costly and diffusive pseudo-transient PDE-based advection. The interpolation produces bounded fields with minimal numerical diffusion. However, it may violate the desired conservation of global properties. Thus, a subsequent optimization step restores conservation while preserving physical bounds. The presented method provides minimally diffusive remapping of finite element fields of arbitrary order. Moreover, it directly remaps quantities defined at integration points, eliminating the need for projection onto finite element spaces. The approach also mitigates typical challenges associated with synchronizing primal variables and conserved quantities in advection-based remap methods. The proposed optimization-based remap method is evaluated using standard two- and three-dimensional remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Direct interpolation followed by constrained optimization enables minimally diffusive ALE remapping while enforcing physical bounds and global conservation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports high-order hydrodynamics simulations with large mesh displacements while conserving volume, mass, momentum, and total energy.
method: Transfer fields through direct physical-space interpolation rather than PDE-based advection.
Restore global conservation through optimization while preserving physical bounds.
Remap arbitrary-order finite element fields and integration-point quantities without intermediate projection.
infographic.evidence_signal: The method is evaluated on standard 2D and 3D remap benchmarks and full ALE hydrodynamics simulations; the abstract provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The scalability and computational cost of the conservation-restoring optimization require assessment for large production simulations.
infographic.paper_title: Remap for ALE Hydrodynamics via Direct Interpolation and Constraint Optimization

title: Trapping and Fracture of Particles in Three-Sphere Ball-Milling Collisions
authors: Ziyi Cui, Qiong Zhang, Suwei Liu, Richard M. Lueptow
abstract: We numerically investigate the collision and fracture processes of ball milling based on a minimal model of a three-sphere geometry using discrete element method (DEM) simulations combined with Christensen-type and Weibull-type normalized fracture criteria. The outcome of the brittle target particle (ejected versus trapped, fractured versus intact) depends on the impact geometry and velocity. We develop a reduced three-sphere collision description in which trapping is governed by impact geometry and friction, while fracture inside the trapping regime is evaluated from DEM output using stress-based and contact-force-based normalized criteria. The trapping regime follows a closed-form geometric condition, while the critical conditions for fracture vary with impact angle, obliquity angle, impact velocity, and particle size ratio. Head-on collisions with larger size ratios require lower critical impact velocities for fracture.

infographic.key_insight: A minimal three-sphere model separates geometry- and friction-controlled particle trapping from fracture, with head-on impacts requiring lower fracture velocities at larger particle size ratios.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model can help guide ball-milling impact conditions toward particle capture and breakage rather than ejection.
method: Simulate three-sphere collisions using the discrete element method (DEM).
Determine trapping with a closed-form geometric condition accounting for friction.
Evaluate fracture using Christensen-type stress and Weibull-type contact-force normalized criteria.
infographic.evidence_signal: DEM results show that particle outcomes and fracture thresholds depend on impact angle, obliquity, velocity, and particle size ratio.
infographic.watch_item: The reduced three-sphere model may not capture collective interactions in a full mill, and the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Trapping and Fracture of Particles in Three-Sphere Ball-Milling Collisions

title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
authors: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj
abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.

infographic.key_insight: Exact boundary and initial constraints enable PINNs to identify the shear piezoelectric coefficient e15 accurately from sparse, noisy simulated wavefields without tuning boundary or initial-condition penalty weights.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support non-destructive characterization of shear-mode coupling in PMUTs and SAW devices, potentially replacing dedicated destructive resonance tests.
method: Embed spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers into network outputs to enforce clamped, grounded boundaries and a resting initial state exactly.
Train using coupled electro-elastodynamic equations and observation misfit, with non-dimensional scaling to balance governing coefficients.
Use a quadratic temporal multiplier to reduce early-time electrostatic residuals.
infographic.evidence_signal: On simulated plane-strain PZT-5H data, constrained variants achieved 0.15–0.51% mean e15 error in a six-way comparison; the full formulation achieved 1.19% on finite-element data at 30 dB noise.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to simulated data; experimental robustness and construction of exact constraint functions for complex device geometries remain untested.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints

title: Finite-element reconstruction of molten-zone dynamics and chemical segregation in optical floating-zone grown Ni--Mn--Ga
authors: Denys Musiienko, Taras Kovaliuk, Petr Harcuba, Oleg Heczko, Ross H. Colman
abstract: Homogeneous single-crystal growth of Ni--Mn--Ga magnetic shape-memory alloys is limited by incongruent melting, Mn reactivity, and longitudinal composition segregation. We report a modified optical floating-zone method in which growth is performed inside a transparent sapphire crucible, stabilising the molten zone while preserving optical heating and visual monitoring. The resulting crystals show improved growth reproducibility and controlled macroscopic geometry. To interpret the measured segregation profiles, a transient finite-element heat-transfer model in COMSOL Multiphysics was coupled to an effective molten-zone mass-balance calculation. The model reveals that the local solidification velocity is not fixed by the imposed translation speed but varies strongly as the molten-zone geometry evolves. The calculated solidification-front geometry is independently supported by EBSD analysis of a quenched growth interface, while the coupled mass-balance calculation reproduces the dominant features of the measured composition profiles. These results show that deviations from ideal Scheil--Pfann behaviour arise from the evolving molten-zone geometry and solidification conditions. The experimentally constrained model therefore provides a practical means of reconstructing otherwise inaccessible growth conditions and a basis for optimisation of sapphire-confined floating-zone growth of incongruently melting alloys.

infographic.key_insight: Evolving molten-zone geometry changes local solidification velocity, helping explain chemical segregation in sapphire-confined floating-zone growth of Ni–Mn–Ga.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Sapphire confinement improves growth reproducibility and macroscopic geometry control, while physics-based reconstruction supports optimisation of more compositionally uniform crystals.
method: Grow Ni–Mn–Ga inside a transparent sapphire crucible using optical floating-zone heating.
Couple transient COMSOL finite-element heat transfer to an effective molten-zone mass balance.
Compare reconstructed interface geometry and segregation with EBSD and measured composition profiles.
infographic.evidence_signal: EBSD of a quenched interface independently supports the calculated front geometry, and the coupled model reproduces dominant features of measured composition profiles.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no quantitative prediction errors; the effective mass-balance model may need validation across other growth conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Finite-element reconstruction of molten-zone dynamics and chemical segregation in optical floating-zone grown Ni--Mn--Ga

title: Optimal stability estimates and preasymptotic error analysis of the CIP-FEM for the Helmholtz equation with uniaxial perfectly matched layers
authors: Silin Wen, Yu Du
abstract: We study the uniaxial perfectly matched layer (UPML) problem for the Helmholtz equation in two and three dimensions and establish wavenumber-explicit stability estimates at high wavenumbers. For the full-space UPML problem, we prove the optimal stability estimate with the inf-sup constant satisfying $μ_\infty\eqsim k^{-1}$ for sufficiently large $k$ if the absorption function $σ\in W^{1,\infty}$ is a piecewise-power function of order at least one for which $\|σ'\|_{L^\infty(\{t:0<σ(t)\leqδ_*\})}\leq \varepsilon_*$, where $\varepsilon_*$ and $δ_*$ depend only on the PML parameters. Using this stability estimate, we obtain the optimal inf-sup estimate $μ_L\eqsim k^{-1}$ for the truncated UPML problem. These estimates further yield preasymptotic error estimates for a linear continuous interior penalty finite element method (CIP-FEM). Numerical simulations confirmed the theoretical predictions and demonstrated the effectiveness of CIP-FEM under high-wavenumber conditions.

infographic.key_insight: For high-wavenumber Helmholtz problems, the paper proves optimal inf-sup scaling μ ≍ k⁻¹ for full-space and truncated uniaxial perfectly matched layers, enabling preasymptotic CIP-FEM error estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results support reliable finite-element simulation of high-frequency wave propagation using absorbing layers to truncate unbounded domains.
method: Analyze full-space UPML stability in two and three dimensions.
Transfer optimal stability estimates to truncated UPML domains.
Derive preasymptotic error estimates for linear continuous interior penalty FEM.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations confirm the theoretical predictions and demonstrate CIP-FEM effectiveness at high wavenumbers, though the abstract reports no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The stability guarantees require sufficiently large wavenumbers and a prescribed piecewise-power absorption profile with controlled derivatives where absorption is small.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal stability estimates and preasymptotic error analysis of the CIP-FEM for the Helmholtz equation with uniaxial perfectly matched layers

title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity
authors: Leonilson Toffoli Pedrini, Maycoln Conci, Rafael Marin Ferro
abstract: Periodic composites with cohesive interfaces and matrix plasticity require nonlinear cell solutions in multiscale analysis. Process-zone condensation eliminates the linear elastic remainder of the cell by a Schur complement, retaining all interfacial and process-zone internal variables. Influence matrices recover macroscopic stress and consistent tangent. One back-substitution per increment checks that the matrix outside the retained zone remains elastic. While this holds, the reduction is exact relative to the full discretisation, also with a plastic matrix, and requires no training. In an E-glass/epoxy cell, eight of nine two-dimensional paths agree with the full cell to 1e-11 in stress and tangent; the check flags the ninth. Three paths on each of two three-dimensional meshes need zone expansion. Excluding setup and checks, two-dimensional path timings show an aggregate speed-up of 3.3; certified three-dimensional zones show none. In adaptive finite element squared (FE$^2$) simulations of a perforated plate, the reduced solver reproduces the full-cell response within solver tolerances, 1.51 times faster for glass/polypropylene and slower for glass/epoxy. Independent Ansys models agree to below 1e-3 in cell stress and about 0.6% in plate reactions, although local damage and plasticity onsets differ. The advantage depends on zone size, active set and adaptation costs.

infographic.key_insight: Process-zone condensation reproduces the full discretized cell response without training while the eliminated matrix region remains elastic.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method can accelerate FE² analysis of composites with fibre–matrix debonding and matrix plasticity while preserving stress and consistent-tangent accuracy.
method: Schur-condense the linear elastic remainder, retaining interface and process-zone internal variables.
Recover macroscopic stress and consistent tangent using influence matrices.
Check the eliminated matrix region by back-substitution each increment; expand the retained zone when needed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eight of nine 2D paths matched full-cell stress and tangent to 1e-11, with the ninth flagged; aggregate 2D speed-up was 3.3× excluding setup and checks, while plate FE² achieved 1.51× for glass/polypropylene.
infographic.watch_item: Speed-up depends on zone size, active set and adaptation costs: certified 3D zones showed no gain, and glass/epoxy plate FE² was slower.
infographic.paper_title: Process-zone condensation: a discretization-exact reduced cell model for FE$^2$ analysis of composites with fibre-matrix debonding and matrix plasticity

title: A Second-Order Semi-Implicit Projection Time-Stepping Scheme for the Shallow-Water Equations on the Sphere Using Compatible Finite Elements
authors: Karina Kowalczyk, Colin Cotter
abstract: We propose a second-order, semi-implicit time-stepping scheme for the shallow-water equations on the sphere discretised with compatible finite elements. The scheme splits the advection operator from the wave operator, applying a DG-upwind SSPRK3 method to the advection part and an $H(\text{div})$-conforming implicit discretisation to the wave part, solved efficiently via hybridisation. The scheme follows a three-step symmetric splitting: an explicit half-step, a full advection step, and an implicit half-step that simultaneously projects the velocity back into the $H(\text{div})$ space. This symmetry guarantees global second-order accuracy and confines the stability restriction to the CFL condition of the advection step alone. The time-step can therefore be extended beyond this limit by subcycling the advection step without additional implicit solves. The method is implemented in Firedrake and validated against a standard suite of spherical shallow-water benchmarks, demonstrating stable results for Courant numbers up to 1 (with two advection subcycles) with second-order finite elements, second-order convergence, and good parallel scaling.

infographic.key_insight: A symmetric semi-implicit projection scheme achieves second-order shallow-water time integration on the sphere while restricting stability by advection rather than fast waves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports larger time steps for spherical geophysical flow simulations, with advection subcycling requiring no additional implicit solves.
method: Use compatible finite elements to separate advection and wave dynamics.
Apply an explicit half-step, a DG-upwind SSPRK3 advection step, and an implicit half-step that projects velocity into H(div).
Solve the implicit wave system efficiently through hybridisation in Firedrake.
infographic.evidence_signal: Standard spherical shallow-water benchmarks show second-order convergence, stable results at Courant numbers up to 1 with two advection subcycles and second-order finite elements, and good parallel scaling.
infographic.watch_item: Reported stability is benchmark-specific; advection subcycling still must respect its CFL restriction and adds explicit computational work.
infographic.paper_title: A Second-Order Semi-Implicit Projection Time-Stepping Scheme for the Shallow-Water Equations on the Sphere Using Compatible Finite Elements

title: A Finite Element Model for Fluid--Poroelastic Structure Interaction with Dissipative Interface
authors: Mohammad Jannesari, Francesco Costanzo
abstract: This paper extends our prior work on interface conditions between two poroelastic domains to the case when a poroelastic domain interacts with a pure fluid. The porous medium is assumed to be deformable and modeled following mixture theory. When not in a mixture, each constituent of the porous domain is assumed to be incompressible. An arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian formulation is developed for both the fluid and porous domains. The fluid velocity and pressure fields are allowed to be discontinuous across the pure fluid/porous domain interface. A globally continuous displacement field is defined to represent both the deformation of the solid skeleton of the poroelastic medium and the mesh motion in the pure fluid domain. As an interface condition, the continuity of the normal component of the filtration velocity is enforced via a Lagrange multiplier. The mixture momentum jump condition is implemented so as to transfer the traction from the fluid side to the porous domain. A dissipative behavior is attributed to the interface, and the jump condition for the fluid momentum, derived from Hamilton's principle, incorporates this prescribed behavior. The model implementation is verified using the method of manufactured solutions, and a sample problem is solved to compare an inert interface with a fully dissipative one. The results show satisfactory convergence rates, while the proposed model successfully reproduces the analytical solution of a benchmark problem using conventional jump conditions. Furthermore, the findings highlight the significant influence of the selected interface model on the behavior of the system.

infographic.key_insight: A finite element model couples pure fluid flow with a deformable poroelastic medium while capturing interface dissipation that significantly affects system behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation supports simulations of fluid–porous structure interaction where interface transport and traction transfer influence deformation and flow.
method: Use mixture theory and an arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian formulation for fluid and poroelastic domains.
Allow discontinuous fluid velocity and pressure across the interface, with a globally continuous displacement field.
Enforce normal filtration-velocity continuity through a Lagrange multiplier and incorporate dissipative momentum jump conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured-solution tests showed satisfactory convergence, a benchmark reproduced an analytical solution, and a sample problem compared inert and fully dissipative interfaces.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports numerical verification but no experimental validation; interface dissipation must be chosen carefully because it strongly influences predictions.
infographic.paper_title: A Finite Element Model for Fluid--Poroelastic Structure Interaction with Dissipative Interface

title: OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment
authors: Sherry Choi, Sitao Sunny Li, Joseph Romero, Lillian Chin, Ashwin G. Ramayya, Allison M. Okamura
abstract: Motor responses evoked by noxious stimulation are used to assess neurological function in hospitalized patients with disorders of consciousness. In standard bedside assessments, these stimuli are applied manually, resulting in substantial variation in force, duration, frequency, and location. Here, we present OUCH (Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic stimulation), a wrist-worn device that uses pneumatic actuation to deliver noxious mechanical stimuli. OUCH combines stacked pneumatic pouch actuators, a rigid indenter, and a compliant spacer designed to buckle at a set load, so that the indenter contacts the skin only during actuation. We characterize the device using blocked force tests, clinician evaluation, finite element analysis, and a deformable pressure testbed, and benchmark it against a commercially available handheld pressure algometer. At 200 kPa pouch inflation pressure, our indenter concentrated its load into an estimated contact pressure of 18,500 kPa, over 25 times that of the algometer tip, while requiring less total force. On the deformable testbed, it localized deformation near the surface, while deformation at depth remained comparable to the algometer. As a result, in preliminary perceptual testing, our indenter elicited discomfort at approximately 89% lower applied force than the algometer, demonstrating the feasibility of evoking discomfort with a compact, wearable soft actuator. These results show that combining pneumatic actuation with designed contact geometry enables controlled, repeatable noxious stimulation at the wrist, providing a foundation for objective neurological assessment.

infographic.key_insight: OUCH combines pneumatic actuation with a focused indenter to evoke discomfort at approximately 89% lower applied force than a handheld pressure algometer in preliminary testing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A compact wrist-worn device could standardize mechanical stimulation for neurological assessment while reducing reliance on variable manual application.
method: Stacked pneumatic pouch actuators drive a rigid indenter.
A compliant spacer buckles at a set load, allowing skin contact only during actuation.
Finite element analysis and physical testing characterize contact mechanics and tissue deformation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation included blocked-force tests, clinician evaluation, finite element analysis, a deformable testbed, and preliminary perceptual testing; at 200 kPa inflation, estimated contact pressure reached 18,500 kPa—over 25 times the algometer tip's pressure.
infographic.watch_item: Preliminary discomfort results do not establish clinical assessment accuracy or repeated-use skin safety in patients with disorders of consciousness.
infographic.paper_title: OUCH: Objective, Uniform, Controlled Haptic Stimulation for Automated Neurological Assessment

title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning
authors: Zhuoli Ouyang, Changxi Chi, Siyuan Li, Tailin Wu
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs. Conversely, confining updates to a low-dimensional subspace reduces variance but discards critical high-dimensional information, degrading performance. This creates a fundamental dilemma: full-space optimization is informative but has high variance, while subspace optimization has low variance but loses information. To break this trade-off, we propose ENGINE (Endogenous Variational MultiScale). Inspired by computational mechanics, we adapt static Variational MultiScale (VMS) theory to dynamic optimization, treating low- and high-dimensional spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales. Through a multigrid-style V-cycle, ENGINE alternates between spaces, dynamically probing fine-grained information in the high-dimensional space and injecting it to correct the efficient low-dimensional sampling process. Under appropriate assumptions, statistical analysis characterizes variance reduction and correction of curvature-induced bias, and convergence analysis establishes a stationarity bound for the corrected coarse updates. Evaluations on standard LLM benchmarks show that ENGINE achieves higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing ZO methods, achieving up to a $2.61\times$ speed-up in forward passes with zero additional peak memory overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/ENGINE.

infographic.key_insight: ENGINE uses high-dimensional probes to correct low-dimensional zeroth-order updates, reducing the trade-off between gradient variance and information loss in LLM fine-tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It transfers variational multiscale ideas from computational mechanics to memory-efficient LLM optimization.
method: Treat low-dimensional and full-parameter spaces as resolved coarse and unresolved fine scales.
Alternate between scales through a multigrid-style V-cycle.
Inject fine-scale information into coarse updates to reduce variance and curvature-induced bias.
infographic.evidence_signal: On standard LLM benchmarks, the abstract reports higher accuracy and faster convergence than existing zeroth-order methods, with up to 2.61× speed-up in forward passes and no additional peak memory overhead.
infographic.watch_item: The theoretical guarantees depend on assumptions, and the abstract does not specify benchmark-level variability or practical subspace-selection requirements.
infographic.paper_title: ENGINE: Endogenous Variational MultiScale Optimization for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning

title: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning
authors: Nishanth Anand, Doina Precup
abstract: Continual Reinforcement Learning (CRL) agents struggle to adapt to new situations while retaining prior knowledge, leading to a stability-plasticity trade-off. One approach to solving this problem is by using complementary learning systems: one for slow, long-term learning and another for quick, transient adaptation. Anand & Precup (2023) instantiated this idea using permanent and transient value functions, but used the same features in both systems. Intuitively, long-term learning should rely more on parametric representations for broad generalization, while transient learning would be best served by non-parametric representations for situation-specific adaptation. In this paper, we explore this idea both theoretically and empirically. By introducing a novel non-parametric approximation for estimating the transient value function in complex tasks, we demonstrate that our method enables online learning and outperforms competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic, underscoring the effectiveness of our system-level decomposition.

infographic.key_insight: Separating permanent parametric representations from transient non-parametric representations helps continual reinforcement learning balance knowledge retention with rapid adaptation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This architecture may inform adaptive engineering control, but the abstract provides no solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling validation.
method: Decompose value estimation into permanent and transient components.
Use parametric representations for long-term generalization.
Introduce a non-parametric transient value approximation for online, situation-specific adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical and empirical investigation, with performance exceeding competitive baselines on image-based tasks and Craftax-Classic.
infographic.watch_item: Memory and computational scaling of the non-parametric component require scrutiny; the abstract gives no resource-cost measurements.
infographic.paper_title: Permanent and Transient Representations for Continual Reinforcement Learning

title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning
authors: Tom Saliencro, Wen-Hsuan Liu, Rohan Desai, Amara Okonkwo, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

infographic.key_insight: BISECT counters spectral starvation in continual LoRA learning by splitting a fixed low-rank budget between shared invariant features and task-specific novelty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For engineering vision workflows with sequentially arriving tasks, BISECT offers a potential adaptation strategy without added inference parameters or FLOPs, though solid-mechanics applications are not evaluated.
method: Extract invariant directions from dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix.
Build an orthogonal novelty block using generalized Rayleigh whitening and complement projection.
Fold trained updates into the frozen backbone, scaling invariant atoms by current-to-joint Rayleigh ratios and retaining novelty atoms at unit gain.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that historical null tails capture only 5.5% of incoming-task variance and that BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines across eight incremental settings on five vision datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Training-time costs and numerical stability of Gram-matrix estimation and generalized Rayleigh whitening are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning

title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
authors: Wen-Hsuan Liu, Amara Okonkwo, Tom Saliencro, Rohan Desai, Maya Lindqvist
abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations. Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks. At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.

infographic.key_insight: RASP separates reading from learning: inference uses all LoRA atoms, while training updates only a sparse subset within one fixed-size adapter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support memory-bounded continual adaptation of engineering vision systems, but the abstract reports no solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling validation.
method: A scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-q unlocked atoms for gradient updates while inference retains all r atoms.
A Frobenius Gram-coherence penalty separates active output directions from non-updated directions.
Router activation histories and atom spectral norms guide Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, the abstract reports matching or surpassing branch-expanding LoRA learners with a strictly constant parameter footprint.
infographic.watch_item: Long-horizon capacity under progressive atom locking remains unclear; the abstract provides no quantitative saturation analysis.
infographic.paper_title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
